title: Enterprise Onboarding, Escalation, Integration & QBR Playbook
author: Jordan Lee
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference’s standard operating procedures for enterprise onboarding, post-integration escalation, ongoing support, known issues and workarounds, and the Quarterly Business Review (QBR) / health-check cadence. It is intended for Customer Success Managers (CSMs), Support Engineers, Solutions Engineers, and SREs executing or supporting enterprise customers.

Scope

- New enterprise customers onboarding to Redwood Hosted / Dedicated / Private deployments.
- Integration activities that exercise the API, routing policies, and deployment-specific network configurations.
- Ongoing operational health checks and the standard QBR deliverable set.
- Escalation flows for customer-impacting incidents and product regressions.

Key goals

1. Reduce time-to-value: target production-ready integration within 2–4 weeks for standard integrations.
2. Clear ownership: define RACI for every onboarding step.
3. Fast, predictable escalations: SLAs and routing for P0–P3 issues.
4. Data-driven QBRs: metrics tied to availability, latency, cost, and model quality.

Roles & responsibilities

- Customer Success Manager (CSM): single-threaded customer lead; owns project plan, requirements, and QBRs.
- Solutions Engineer (SE): leads technical kickoff, sample prompts, and integration verification.
- Support Engineer (L1/L2): triage issues, communicate status, and escalate to Eng/SRE when required.
- SRE / Eng: owns platform incidents, capacity, and known-issue fixes.
- Security/Compliance (when applicable): validates private deployment controls, audit logging, and KMS integration.

Onboarding phases (high level)

1) Pre-kickoff (Sales → CSM handoff)
   - Deliverables: legal, security questionnaire, initial success criteria, datasets for evals.
   - Action: CSM schedules Kickoff and introduces SE and Support Owners.

2) Kickoff (Week 0)
   - Agenda: success criteria, auth & network requirements, data residency, SLAs, timeline.
   - Output: agreed project plan, integration owner list, and access matrix.

3) Integration & Verification (Week 1–3)
   - Tasks: API key exchange, test prompts, rate-limit configuration, routing policy setup, and latency/cost baseline run.
   - Validation: pass smoke tests and 95th-percentile latency under agreed threshold.

4) Go-live & Monitoring (Week 3–4)
   - Tasks: production key rotation, canary rollout if applicable, enable tracing and cost alerts.
   - Output: Production readiness sign-off from CSM, SE, and customer engineering lead.

5) Post-go-live & QBR cadence
   - Weekly health checks for first 4 weeks, then transition to monthly checks and quarterly QBRs.

Integration checklist (table)

| Item | Owner | Target | Completion criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| Signed SOW & security questionnaire | CSM | Day -7 | Documents uploaded to customer folder |
| API key provisioning and scopes | SE/Customer | Day 0 | Valid test key returns 200 on /v1/generate |
| Network allowlist & VPN config (Private/Dedicated) | Customer/SRE | Day 0–3 | Successful ping / health check from Redwood probes |
| Sample prompts & eval set | SE/Customer | Day 1–5 | Quality baseline agreed (pass rate >= 90%) |
| Rate limits & quotas configured | CSM/SE | Day 2 | Throttling validated under load |
| Observability hooks (tracing, logs, cost) | SRE/SE | Day 3 | Dashboards show incoming requests and token breakdown |

Escalation process

Severity definitions and expected response/initial action times:
- P0 (Platform outage / data loss): 1 hour initial response; continuous updates every 30 minutes until resolution.
- P1 (Customer-impacting performance regression or correctness regression): 4 hour initial response; updates every 1–2 hours.
- P2 (Partial loss of functionality, intermittent errors): 8 business hour response; daily updates.
- P3 (Informational / minor issues): 1 business day response; weekly updates until resolved.

Escalation matrix (contacts and flow):
1) L1 Support (Support Engineers): triage and attempt remediation within SLA.
2) L2 Support / SE: deeper log analysis, reproduce and collect traces.
3) SRE / Runtime Team: capacity, routing, kernel issues.
4) Eng (Model/Backend): code-level fixes, regressions, release rollbacks.

Communication channels:
- Primary: Support ticket + Slack (customer-specific channel where available).
- P0/P1: Create incident in PagerDuty and open a shared Slack bridge; CSM responsible for customer comms.

Escalation checklist:
1) Validate customer environment and collect: request_id, timestamps, sample payloads, model/variant, deployment region, p50/p95 latency and token counts.
2) Attach logs and trace links; if Private, obtain secure bundle per data policy.
3) Assign severity and inform SRE/Eng on-call if severity >= P1.
4) Initiate rollback or scaling action if applicable; document impact and ETA.

Known issues & standard workarounds (examples)

- Issue: Elevated p95 latency for long-context prompts on GPU T4 pool.
  Workaround: Switch to Foundry or a larger GPU class (e.g., A10/A100) for that workload; enable prefix KV caching and reduce batch size.

- Issue: 429 rate-limited errors during burst traffic.
  Workaround: Implement client-side exponential backoff, enable burst capacity option on Dedicated, or request temporary quota increase via CSM.

- Issue: Model quality regression after rolling custom quantized variant.
  Workaround: Pin to last-known-good model variant and create regression ticket to Model Ops for evaluation and rollback.

Support process & SLAs

- Ticket intake: all customer issues should be logged in the support portal with required metadata: customer ID, environment, request IDs, example payloads.
- Target SLAs: initial response per severity (see Escalation process). Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) targets: P0 <= 1 hour, P1 <= 4 hours. Mean time to resolve (MTTR) targets vary by severity and root cause.
- Escalation ownership: CSM owns customer comms and coordinates cross-functional triage. L2/SE owns technical reproductions. SRE/Eng owns fixes or rollbacks.

Health checks & QBR (templates and metrics)

Weekly health check (first month) - checklist:
- Usage: total tokens, request count, peak QPS.
- Errors: 5xx rate, 429 rate, client error rate.
- Latency: p50 / p95 / p99 for generation and embedding APIs.
- Cost: cost per 1K tokens and trend vs baseline.
- Model quality: sample prompt regressions, quality score (customer eval).
- Operational: autoscale events, capacity throttles, incidents.

Quarterly QBR template (agenda):
1) Executive summary: adoption highlights, business outcomes.
2) Health summary: uptime, incident summary, risk areas.
3) Performance & cost: latency, throughput, cost efficiency trends.
4) Quality & accuracy: prompt set regressions, A/B results.
5) Roadmap & feature asks: product changes relevant to customer.
6) Action items & next steps: owner, priority, target date.

Suggested QBR KPIs (to include in dashboard):
- Uptime (monthly): target >= 99.9% for hosted API.
- Error rate (5xx): target <= 0.1%.
- Latency p95: target aligned to customer SLO (commonly < 800ms for short prompts).
- Token cost per 1K: baseline and trend.
- Model quality pass rate on curated prompt set: target >= 90% (customer-defined).

- Integration test checklist (copyable)

Appendix: quick copyable checklists

- Pre-kickoff checklist: SOW, security questionnaire, primary contacts.
- Kickoff agenda: goals, network, auth, observability, timeline.
- Go-live checklist: production keys, canary plan, rollback plan, post-go-live monitoring.

If you have a new customer scenario that diverges from this playbook (e.g., air-gapped on-prem deployment, regulatory data residency constraints), escalate to the Security & Compliance reviewer and the Private Deployments lead for a tailored runbook.
